data.title: DOJ ditches lawsuit that sought to pause certification of Alaska's U.S. Senate election
data.description:
16:28
News Story
  • Election 2026
  • Justice

DOJ abandons lawsuit that sought to pause certification of Alaska’s US Senate election

Federal attorneys tell appeals court that their challenge has become moot by the results of the election, which will be certified next week

By James Brooks - November 19, 2026 4:28 pm

U.S. Attorney General Todd Blanche appears at his confirmation hearing in front of the Senate Judiciary Committee on Capitol Hill in early 2026. (Photo by Eric Lee/Getty Images)

Attorneys representing the U.S. Department of Justice told the federal 9th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals on Thursday that they are no longer pursuing a lawsuit against the Alaska Division of Elections over its handling of the state’s U.S. Senate election.

In a new filing, attorneys for the federal agency said “this case has become moot,” a statement signaling they will not oppose the state certifying Democratic candidate Mary Peltola as the winner of the election.

On Wednesday, Alaska Division of Elections Director Carol Beecher said she intends to certify the election, including Peltola’s victory over incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Dan Sullivan, next week.

According to preliminary results through Wednesday, Peltola’s margin over Sullivan is greater than the number of first-choice votes cast for Sullivan and all other candidates combined. When seated in Congress, she will join a 56-person Democratic Senate majority elected amid a nationwide surge of support for Democratic candidates.

Last month, the federal government, at the urging of President Donald Trump, sued the state and asked a federal judge to issue an order that would preclude elections officials from certifying Peltola as the election winner while it investigated whether the presence of independent candidate Dan J. Sullivan confused Alaska voters.

Trump administration sues to block Alaska’s US Senate election result if Peltola wins

U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason dismissed the suit, saying the federal government lacked standing, but the Department of Justice appealed to the 9th Circuit.

The League of Women Voters of Alaska and the national organization Common Cause, arguing on the appeal, asked the appellate court to issue a summary order upholding Gleason’s decision and asked the appellate judges to punish the federal attorneys that filed the case.

“The legal theory advanced by the United States here is embarrassing and indefensible,” wrote attorneys from the American Civil Liberties Union, which represented the two groups. “The Court should summarily affirm and then order the attorneys for the United States to explain why they or their client should not be sanctioned for pursuing a frivolous appeal.”

On Thursday, the federal government responded, saying that instead of summarily upholding Gleason’s decision, the appeals court should vacate it, erasing it from the books entirely, because it is now moot.

Alaskans have now voted, the federal government said, and ballots for Dan J. Sullivan are mixed with other ballots, making it impossible to determine who voted for Dan J. Sullivan.

“The United States therefore reluctantly acknowledges that there no longer exists any means of determin[ing] whether votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan,” the federal attorneys wrote.

In late October, the New York Times reported that Dan J. Sullivan had been recruited by Democratic campaigners who sought to spoil the re-election campaign of Sen. Dan Sullivan. 

“The purpose of this lawsuit,” federal attorneys wrote, “was always to make sure that voters had the opportunity to cast a vote accurately reflecting their choice of candidate, notwithstanding the confusion caused (and intended to be caused) by Daniel J. Sullivan’s campaign, egged on by Peltola’s.”

While the civil lawsuit is winding down, a separate criminal investigation is continuing. The Anchorage Daily News reported on Wednesday that both the Alaska Bureau of Investigation and FBI are continuing to investigate whether any laws were violated by Dan J. Sullivan’s recruitment as a candidate.

data.title: White House national cyber director is leaving his post
data.description:
Trump ousts cyber director after tech outages spark criticism

By Courtney Rozen
Fri, November 20, 2026 at 1:21 AM UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Courtney Rozen

WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross was "fired" from his job, ‌a person close to the White House said ‌on Thursday, days after tech outages hit US air travel, banking ​and national security systems.

Cairncross oversaw cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government. Department of Defense Chief Information Officer Kirsten Davies will assume the position temporarily, according to the ‌source.

Advertisement

"The president fully ⁠supported firing Sean Cairncross from his position," said the person, who spoke on condition of ⁠anonymity.

Cairncross declined to comment on his departure.

Technology-related outages have hit regularly over the last week, including a nationwide halt ​to ​air travel, a Microsoft outage ​that hit email services ‌and a temporary disruption to the US National Security Agency's network.

The Trump administration has faced criticism over its response to the outages. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the disruptions to critical systems over the past ‌week were separate service outages ​associated with maintenance and technical changes ​and not a ​coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Cairncross was an executive ‌at the Republican National Committee ​before assuming the ​cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by the US Senate, which will ​be controlled by ‌Democrats beginning in January.

(Reporting by Courtney Rozen and ​Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by Caitlin Webber, ​John Mair and Lincoln Feast.)

data.title: White House national cyber director is leaving his post
data.description:
White House national cyber director Cairncross leaving his post

By Courtney Rozen
Thu, November 19, 2026 at 11:53 PM UTC
1 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Courtney Rozen

WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - White House national cyber director Sean Cairncross is leaving his post, a ‌White House official said on Thursday, marking the latest ‌departure from the Trump administration following Republican losses in this month's midterm elections.

Cairncross, ​who leads the Office of the National Cyber Director that coordinates cybersecurity policy and strategy across the federal government, did not want to serve another two years and was leaving now to ‌give the White House ⁠time to secure Senate confirmation for his successor before Democrats take control of Congress in January, Axios ⁠reported earlier.

Advertisement

Cairncross' departure was amicable, Axios reported.

President Donald Trump's Republican Party lost its majority in the Senate and House of Representatives ​in this ​month's US midterm elections.

The news ​of the departure comes after ‌tech outages that have hit US air travel, banking and national security systems in recent days.

The Trump administration has faced criticism over its response to the outages. The top US intelligence official said on Wednesday the series of disruptions to critical systems ‌over the past week was not ​a coordinated or state-sponsored attack.

Top US ​officials have repeatedly said ​the outages are separate from each other and ‌not related to any cyberattacks.

Cairncross ​was an executive ​at the Republican National Committee before assuming the cyber director role. His successor will need to be confirmed by ​the US Senate, which ‌will be controlled by Democrats beginning in January.

(Reporting by ​Courtney Rozen and Kanishka Singh in Washington; Editing by ​Caitlin Webber and John Mair)

data.title: Senate Republicans quash resolution curbing Trump's Iran war powers
data.description:
Backing Trump, US Senate Republicans block Iran war resolution

By Patricia Zengerle
Thu, November 19, 2026 at 9:27 PM UTC
2 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

By Patricia Zengerle

WASHINGTON, Nov 19 (Reuters) - US Senate Republicans on Thursday rejected legislation directing President Donald Trump to end the war in Iran or obtain Congress' approval to continue, backing the president weeks ‌after sweeping defeats in midterm elections largely tied to Americans' frustration with the conflict.

The Senate voted 51 ‌to 48, largely along party lines, to defeat a war powers resolution that had previously passed the House of Representatives.

Advertisement

The US Constitution says that ​only Congress, not the president, can declare war, and Democrats have argued that Trump may have pulled the country into a long conflict by failing to spell out a clear strategy.

Only three Republicans - Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska and Rand Paul of Kentucky - voted with Democrats in favor of the resolution. One Democrat, John Fetterman of Pennsylvania, voted with ‌Republicans against it.

The vote was the first ⁠on the conflict since Democratic victories in the midterm elections on November 3. Trump's fellow Republicans, who rarely break with the president, stood behind him in support of the US-Israeli war ⁠on Iran that started on February 28.

Just 31% of Americans approve of the US war on Iran, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll conducted November 13-16.

It was the 21st vote in Congress on a war powers resolution since the war began. Democrats said ​they filed ​the measure to put Republicans on the record as supporting ​the war.

SHOWDOWN LOOMS IN 2027

Democrats will control large ‌majorities in the House and Senate next year, and party leaders have pledged to make ending the war a top priority once they take over on January 3, setting the stage for a potential showdown with Trump.

Democratic Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia, who has called repeatedly for Congress to take back its control over declarations of war, said the midterm election result reflected Americans' unhappiness about the war, and higher prices for food, fuel and other goods linked to ‌the conflict.

"Its unpopularity was made absolutely, manifestly clear in the election ​results of November 3," Kaine said in a speech before the vote ​appealing for yes votes.

Democrats made affordability a theme ​of the election campaign.

Democrats have also balked at the cost of the foreign conflict, at a ‌time when Republicans have been cutting domestic programs ​like health insurance subsidies and ​free school lunches.

Pentagon data in late October showed that the US military had spent over $47 billion to prosecute the war, more than 25% higher than the Defense Department's estimate in July.

The latest resolution had passed the ​House in mid-September by 220-204, reflecting lawmakers' ‌growing unhappiness with the months-long conflict weeks before the midterms.

A similar measure passed both the Senate and ​House earlier this year, but the Trump administration ignored it, saying it was not legally binding.

(Reporting ​by Patricia Zengerle; Editing by Don Durfee and Alistair Bell)

data.title: Anthropic shares open for trading at $111.50, spiking more than 30% above IPO price
data.description:
LIVE Updated 15 mins ago

Anthropic IPO live: Anthropic stock begins trading in record $81B raise with $1.5T valuation

Daniel Howley · Technology Editor
Updated Thu, November 19, 2026 at 11:24 AM PST 1 min read
  • ANT +16.57%

Anthropic (ANT) began trading on Thursday at $111.50 per share, well above its $83 IPO price, giving it a market capitalization of $2 trillion.

The company, which was founded in 2021, raised a record-breaking $81.3 billion in its initial public offering at a valuation of $1.5 trillion.

CEO Dario Amodei and president Daniela Amodei were at the Nasdaq in Times Square to ring the opening bell ahead of the first trade, with Dario saying that safety will be key to how AI is developed and deployed.

Daniela Amodei, meanwhile, addressed concerns about AI growth, saying, "To anyone watching who is uneasy about AI or unsure what it will mean for you. This technology needs you. Not your trust, not your use, but your voice."

Anthropic, which Yahoo Finance named its Company of the Year for 2026, reported in its most recent amended S-1 that its third-quarter revenue climbed to $17 billion, a 12x year over year increase.

Now the market will determine how that risk factors into the company's future prospects.

LIVE 61 updates
  • 15 mins ago
    Daniel Howley

    Anthropic stock sales have 23 lock-up dates

    Anthropic (ANT) has set 23 different lock-up expiration dates for sales of its stock from as early as the initial trading day to as late as the second full trading day after the company releases its Sept. 30, 2027 earnings results.

    The tranches vary in size from 174 million shares to up to 3 billion.

  • 29 mins ago
    Jared Blikre

    The 'Barbenheimer of Finance'

    Users on X are taking note that the release of "Grand Theft Auto VI" and the Anthropic IPO happened on the same day.

  • Today at 6:15 PM UTC
    Jared Blikre

    Anthropic’s first half hour is the worst start for a big IPO since 2008

    The biggest IPO ever drew $15 billion in the first minute. Then the selling started.

    Anthropic (ANT) opened at $111.50, 34% above its $83 IPO price, and slid to about $97 by its 30th minute of trading, a 13% drop. That erased nearly $200 billion in market value, based on the 13.1 billion shares Yahoo Finance counts as implied shares outstanding.

    No big US IPO since 2008 was further below its first trade 30 minutes in, according to a Yahoo Finance review of 1-minute trading data for 21 of them. Coupang (CPNG) came closest at nearly 13%. SpaceX (SPCX) was up almost 10% at the same point in its June debut.

  • Today at 6:06 PM UTC
    Grace O'Donnell

    'Kind of cool': Early Anthropic investor and actor Ashton Kutcher weighs in on IPO

    Ashton Kutcher celebrated Anthropic's blockbuster IPO on Thursday, and with good reason: Kutcher's venture capital firm A-Grade made a $435 million investment in Anthropic that's now worth roughly $7 billion, according to Newsweek.

    With Anthropic now worth well over $1 trillion, Kutcher's stake could make the "That '70s Show" actor a billionaire.

    "People usually see the one deal and think that's the whole thing, but the ones who know realize that it's years of work, micro victories and failures stacked on top of one another," Kutcher wrote on X.

    "Kind of cool when that works out," Kutcher said.

  • Today at 5:58 PM UTC
    Daniel Howley

    Ives says Anthropic IPO provides a 'read on demand' for frontier AI companies

    Yorkville's Dan Ives says Anthropic's (ANTH) market debut offers a look at demand for frontier-lab AI exposure among investors.

    "For the first time a US frontier lab carries a standalone public market price, uncluttered by an ad business or a rocket business," he wrote in a note to investors, referring to Google (GOOG, GOOGL) and SpaceX (SPCX).

    "At a time in which investors are very nervous on the overall tech trade and the Nvidia black cloud moment casts a shadow over the tech sector, Anthropic's debut is a big near-term win for the tech sector and should help restore some investor confidence that the AI Revolution growth thesis is not waning," Ives wrote.

    The analyst admitted that the AI trade is in the midst of a "very turbulent, white-knuckle period," but said it doesn't change his long-term view that companies will spend $3 trillion to $4 trillion on AI capital expenditures in the years ahead.

    Daniel Howley

    Anthropic stock's first trade was worth $12 billion — 34% above its IPO price

    Wall Street waited until nearly noon for Anthropic's first trade. That one print was worth about $12 billion.

    Anthropic (ANT) opened Thursday at $111.50 a share, 34% above its $83 IPO price, as 108 million shares changed hands in the opening trade. That single print was bigger than SpaceX's (SPCX) entire first minute of trading in June, about $9 billion.

    The first full minute was bigger still. About 139 million shares, roughly $15 billion of stock, traded in Anthropic's first 60 seconds, by Yahoo Finance calculations. That's nearly twice SpaceX's first minute, about three times Alibaba's (BABA) in 2014, and about 14% of the 980 million shares sold in the offering.

    The rush capped the biggest IPO ever. Anthropic raised $81.3 billion after pricing above its $70-$78 range, and the opening price valued the company at nearly $2 trillion on a fully diluted basis.

    The 34% opening pop was about three times SpaceX's 11%, though well short of Cerebras' (CBRS) 89% in May. IPOs priced above their marketed range have averaged a 50% first-day gain since 1980, according to data from University of Florida professor Jay Ritter. Read more.

    Everyday investors get 15% allocation in ANT

    Half of the institutional investors were zeroed out to create 15% room for the retail allocation in Anthropic's public listing, according to people familiar with the deal.

    Anthropic and its bankers originally targeted an allocation of up to 20% for retail investors.

    Platforms like Charles Schwab (SCHW) and Fidelity (FIS) lowered their minimum asset thresholds for investors who could ask for shares in the IPO to $50,000 and $25,000, respectively. Meanwhile, Robinhood (HOOD) had no minimum.

  • Today at 4:00 PM UTC
    Brian Sozzi

    3 weird things investors should know about Anthropic

    If you are eyeing a purchase of Anthropic's (ANT) stock on its IPO day today or in the coming days, you will have to accept that this isn't exactly a normal public company.

    Seven somewhat strange founders control all the shots at Anthropic, for one. And two, there is basically a competitor in OpenAI's (OPAI.PVT) ChatGPT doing the same thing as Anthropic.

    But if you dig deeper into Anthropic's business, there are more interesting factoids you will also have to get comfortable with if you want to be a shareholder.

    1. Anthropic has a donation-matching program in which employees can pledge a meaningful portion of their equity awards or the equivalent cash proceeds to a donor-advised fund or other nonprofit organization, and the company then matches those donations with shares of its Class N common stock. The company incurred $2.1 billion in expenses in the first nine months of 2026 related to this program, representing about 6% of total operating expenses. It saw $541 million in these expenses in 2025.

    2. Water is a legitimate risk to Anthropic's ability to grow its business quickly. "Our facilities separately depend on access to reliable water for cooling, which in some regions is scarce, subject to use restrictions, or increasingly costly. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect the availability of the power or water we require, increase our costs, or limit our ability to develop, expand, or operate our data center facilities, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations," the company noted in its S-1 filing.

    3. Anthropic may have to pay for compute whether or not it uses it. The company noted in its S-1 filing, "Our equipment supply framework agreements and similar arrangements may expose us to further risks, including minimum purchase or take-or-pay commitments, price escalation, and obligations that we are unable to align with our actual deployment needs."

data.title: Key takeaways from the historic summit between Trump, Xi and Putin
data.description:
Takeaways from the historic summit between Trump, Xi and Putin

ELAINE KURTENBACH, KANIS LEUNG and AAMER MADHANI
Updated Thu, November 19, 2026 at 3:43 PM UTC
6 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin on Thursday was the first-ever sit-down for the leaders of the three countries.

They started with talk of a shared responsibility for keeping peace as the victors of World War II and as global powers. But post-meeting readouts by the three nations reflected more symbolism than substance.

The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran. It said they agreed on the need for reforms to the United Nations, on increasing oil supplies and on reducing nuclear risks. The statement did not spell out the type and extent of the U.N. reforms the leaders agreed to.

Advertisement

The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, opposing what they called "jurisdiction abuse" by the International Criminal Court, the reports said.

Here are key takeaways from the talks, which lasted over an hour.

China's Xi presided over the summit of 21st century powers

Xi added to China's already burgeoning diplomatic stature merely by hosting the event.

He said the talks with Trump and Putin were positive and fruitful, and that the three nations had aligned views on safeguarding world peace, according to China's Xinhua official news agency.

They agreed major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously and believe differences should be resolved through negotiation and cooperation, Xinhua reported.

"As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace," Xi was quoted as saying. "The seeds planted at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit."

China's insistence that it has the right to recover the democratically governed island of Taiwan, possibly by force, was not addressed in the leaders' broadly worded agreement. China considers that a domestic issue.

China likes to position itself as a different kind of superpower from the U.S. and Russia — one that doesn't get involved in wars and advocates for smaller states, said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.

Beijing's priority was steering the meeting away from specifics, she said. "Beijing wanted to be seen as the adult in the room."

Trump claims a place in history

Trump heralded the leaders' gathering as "really making history" and he suggested to Xi and Putin that together they were shaking things up by ditching the "old school" way adversaries engage.

The White House set low expectations for the talks. But Trump framed them Thursday as only the beginning — a chance to get the conversation rolling on solving some of the world's thorniest issues.

"A lot of wonderful things can come out of this, or at least start," Trump told Putin during a one-on-one meeting prior to their three-way meeting with Xi.

The carefully crafted event was a welcome break for Trump after a couple of rotten weeks for his presidency in which his Republican Party was trounced in the midterm elections, widespread tech outages spooked Americans, and Iran escalated attacks on U.S. allies.

Trump said Iran was on the agenda as was Russia's war against Ukraine. China and Russia carry enormous sway with Tehran and also have been accused by the U.S. of supporting the Islamic Republic.

He reiterated Thursday that he and Xi agree Iran needs to fully reopen the Strait of Hormuz, a critical waterway for world energy supplies that has become a chokepoint since the start of the war. They also agree that Iran cannot obtain a nuclear weapon, Trump said.

But there were no signs that Trump secured any agreements from Xi or Putin to help solve the Iran conflict.

Following the talks, Trump dialed into a meeting in Berlin between U.S. envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy alongside more than 40 European leaders who are supporting Ukraine's war effort.

Trump told the Berlin gathering that he spoke to Xi and Putin about finding a peaceful end to the Ukraine war, Witkoff said.

Putin shares spotlight with Trump and Xi

For Putin, the three-way talks on the sidelines of the APEC summit — and his meetings with both leaders separately earlier — offered a much-coveted chance for the Kremlin leader to signal that he heads a superpower on par with the United States and China.

Trump and Putin found common ground in their opposition to the ICC. The Russian leader is wanted by the ICC under an arrest warrant for his alleged war crimes in Ukraine. The U.S. opposes the ICC's arrest warrant against former Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Putin last attended an APEC summit in 2017. His presence as an honored guest and Russia's status as a top global power — at least at the gathering in Shenzhen — mark a diplomatic breakthrough.

Just before the summit, Russia sent a pair of nuclear-capable Tu-95 bombers on a visit to Vietnam in a reminder of its nuclear might. And as Putin arrived in China, Russian TV zeroed in on an officer in his retinue who was carrying a briefcase with the codes for Moscow's nuclear forces.

Putin addressed Xi as "dear friend" during their talks on Wednesday, and smiled contentedly on Thursday as he shook hands with Trump, who called him "my friend" and boasted about their "great relationship for many years."

Speaking at the start of the three-way talks, Putin underscored the global weight of Russia, China and the U.S. The three nations are "united not only by our status as victors in World War II, but, most importantly, by our shared responsibility for maintaining international peace and security," he said.

They are also among the founders of the United Nations, Putin noted, adding that "we bear responsibility for preserving and strengthening the system of international law."

"Our nations share many common interests regarding the resolution of regional conflicts, including, of course, the conflict in Ukraine," Putin said.

Russia's war in Ukraine featured in Putin's bilateral meetings with Trump and Xi. It wasn't the main topic of the three-way talks, Putin's spokesman Dmitry Peskov said.

The Kremlin released video of the Chinese leader escorting the Russian president to his car at the end of the talks and the two men shaking hands.

"I don't think anyone even expected things to go so well," Putin told Xi as the two men parted ways.

___

Madhani reported from Washington and Leung reported from Hong Kong.

data.title: Trump, Xi and Putin's 'peace declaration' leaves out the wars in Iran and Ukraine
data.description:
Takeaways from the historic summit between Trump, Xi and Putin

ELAINE KURTENBACH, KANIS LEUNG and AAMER MADHANI
Updated Thu, November 19, 2026 at 3:43 PM UTC
5 min read
Add Yahoo as a preferred source to see more of our stories on Google.

SHENZHEN, China (AP) — The meeting between U.S. President Donald Trump, China's Xi Jinping and Russia's Vladimir Putin on Thursday was the first-ever sit-down for the leaders of the three countries.

They started with talk of a shared responsibility for keeping peace as the victors of World War II and as global powers. But post-meeting readouts by the three nations reflected more symbolism than substance.

The "peace declaration" released after their meeting made no mention of Russia's war in Ukraine or the U.S.-led war in Iran. It said they agreed on the need for reforms to the United Nations, on increasing oil supplies and on reducing nuclear risks. The statement did not spell out the type and extent of the U.N. reforms the leaders agreed to.

Advertisement

The three sides also agreed that state officials should enjoy immunity from prosecution, opposing what they called "jurisdiction abuse" by the International Criminal Court, the reports said.

Here are key takeaways from the talks, which lasted over an hour.

Xi added to China's already burgeoning diplomatic stature merely by hosting the event.

He said the talks with Trump and Putin were positive and fruitful, and that the three nations had aligned views on safeguarding world peace, according to China's Xinhua official news agency.

They agreed major powers should take the legitimate security concerns of all countries seriously and believe differences should be resolved through negotiation and cooperation, Xinhua reported.

"As long as dialogue does not stop, doors remain open, there is hope for peace," Xi was quoted as saying. "The seeds planted at today's trilateral meeting will surely take root, sprout, blossom and bear fruit."

China's insistence that it has the right to recover the democratically governed island of Taiwan, possibly by force, was not addressed in the leaders' broadly worded agreement. China considers that a domestic issue.

China likes to position itself as a different kind of superpower from the U.S. and Russia — one that doesn't get involved in wars and advocates for smaller states, said Ruby Osman, a senior policy adviser at London's Tony Blair Institute for Global Change.

data.description:
FIRST ON NBC NEWS
Congress

Sen. Elissa Slotkin fires back at DOJ official over investigation of her political speech

U.S. Attorney Aaron Reitz has suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.
Listen to this article with a free profile
00:0000:00
Add NBC News to Google
Nov. 18, 2026, 8:33 PM EST
By Ryan J. Reilly

WASHINGTON — A Democratic senator repeatedly targeted by the Trump administration for potential prosecution due to her political remarks is firing back at a Trump-appointed Justice Department official over what she called a “baseless” inquiry into her rhetoric about congressional oversight.

Sen. Elissa Slotkin, D-Mich., is one of five Democratic members of Congress who have been the subject of letters that the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, Aaron Reitz, has posted on social media. In one of the letters, which have come under scrutiny from legal experts, Reitz suggested that Slotkin’s comments about congressional oversight potentially acting as a “deterrence message” to people considering joining the Trump administration could amount to a criminal civil rights offense.

“I made those statements consistent with my basic right to freedom of speech, a right that every American enjoys under the First Amendment to the U.S. Constitution,” Slotkin wrote Wednesday in a letter to Reitz obtained by NBC News. “In addition to my First Amendment rights, as a United States Senator, oversight is an important constitutional responsibility.”

“The Constitution’s Speech or Debate clause bars prosecution of a legislator for conducting an investigation or performing other legislative acts,” she wrote. “As such, your threat of investigation is baseless, and you should withdraw your letter immediately.”

Slotkin went on to say that Reitz’s “public threats” violated Justice Department policy, and that his decision to publicly post the letter rather than providing it to her, her attorney or the Senate legal counsel “is evidence that your threat of investigation is more about publicity and your political ambitions than any sort of legitimate inquiry.”

Reitz, 39, previously worked as chief of staff for Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and became U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas over the summer after placing fourth in the Republican primary for state attorney general.

Reitz also posted letters on X to Sen. Elizabeth Warren, D-Mass., Sen. Richard Blumenthal, D-Conn., Rep. Robert Garcia, D-Calif., and Sen. Adam Schiff, D-Calif.

He told NBC News this week that he was “not interested in chilling free speech.”

Slotkin and five other sitting Democratic lawmakers were separately targeted by the Trump administration earlier this year over a video they posted to social media that sought to remind members of the military and intelligence communities that they should not obey unlawful orders. Allies of the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro, tried to indict the six Democrats for their speech in that video, but federal grand jurors unanimously rejected the indictment attempt.

Slotkin’s attorney, Preet Bharara, had previously written a letter to Attorney General Todd Blanche cautioning him against following President Donald Trump’s public instruction to look into Slotkin’s political speech, which he dubbed a “criminal act.”

Blanche has conceded that Slotkin’s words alone were “absolutely not a crime” and said at a press conference last week that there were “no ongoing investigations, criminal investigations, into words that incoming senators or congressmen have said.”
